title: Application of Asepsis to Sterile Procedures and Operating Theatres
path: Application of Asepsis to Sterile Procedures and Operating Theatres

headings.title: Introduction to Asepsis and Infection Control Principles
headings.content: Asepsis means the absence of disease-producing microorganisms. In healthcare, infection control aims to protect patients from healthcare-associated infections, commonly called hospital-acquired infections. Handwashing remains the single most effective way to stop germs from spreading between patients and staff. Standard precautions apply to all patients regardless of their diagnosis, treating all body fluids as potentially infectious.

headings.title: Medical Asepsis Versus Surgical Asepsis
headings.content: Medical asepsis, or clean technique, reduces the number of organisms and prevents their spread. Examples include hand hygiene and routine surface cleaning. Surgical asepsis, or sterile technique, eliminates all microorganisms, including spores, from an object or area. It is mandatory for procedures involving sterile body cavities, such as surgeries and urinary catheter insertions.

headings.title: Operating Theatre Zoning and Environmental Controls
headings.content:
The operating theatre uses strict zoning to control air quality and traffic flow. 
- **Unrestricted zone**: Street clothes are permitted; this includes reception and changing areas.
- **Semi-restricted zone**: Staff must wear surgical scrubs, caps, and shoes; includes corridors and instrument processing rooms.
- **Restricted zone**: Full surgical attire including masks and eye protection is mandatory; includes operating suites where sterile supplies are open.

headings.title: Principles and Rules of Sterile Technique
headings.content: Maintaining sterility requires strict adherence to core physical rules. A sterile field can only touch another sterile item. If a sterile barrier is breached or punctured, the entire field is considered contaminated. Any item falling below waist level or falling out of direct vision is contaminated. Sterile personnel must face each other and avoid turning their backs to the sterile table.

headings.title: Surgical Scrubbing, Gowning, and Gloving
headings.content: Surgical hand scrubbing removes transient flora and reduces resident skin flora for the duration of the procedure. Hands and arms are scrubbed using an antiseptic agent, holding hands higher than the elbows so water drains downward. When donning sterile gowns and gloves, closed gloving technique provides an extra layer of safety by keeping bare skin from touching the outside of the glove.

headings.title: Sterilization and Preparation of Instruments
headings.content: Instruments must undergo thorough decontamination, cleaning, and inspection before sterilization. Autoclaving uses steam under pressure to destroy all microbial life, including bacterial endospores. Chemical indicators and biological tests verify that the sterilizer reached the required temperature and pressure parameters.

headings.title: Maintaining the Sterile Field During Procedures
headings.content: Once established, the sterile field must be continuously monitored. Sterile tables should be set up immediately before use and never left unattended. Fluid splashes across sterile drapes create a pathway for bacteria through a process called wicking, immediately contaminating the field.

headings.title: Role of the Scrub and Circulating Nurse in Asepsis Enforcement
headings.content: The surgical team shares responsibility for maintaining asepsis. The scrub nurse remains sterile, manages instruments, and tracks sponges. The circulating nurse remains non-sterile, coordinates room traffic, opens supplies using aseptic technique, and monitors environmental safety. Both nurses have the professional duty to speak up immediately if anyone breaks sterile technique.

headings.title: Post-Procedure Decontamination and Waste Management
headings.content: After surgery, proper waste segregation prevents injuries and infection transmission. Sharps like needles and blades go into puncture-resistant safety boxes. Contaminated linens go into designated bags. Instruments are pre-rinsed or wiped of gross debris and sent to central sterilization in closed containers.
